questiontext.text:
A student differentiates using the power rule. Read their working carefully.

[[ if test="notn=1" ]]

They want \( f'(x) \) for \( f(x) = {@expr@} \), and write:

\[ f'(x) = {@ev(L1s,simp=false)@} = {@buggy_final@}. \][[/ if ]] [[ if test="notn=2" ]]

They want \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \) for \( y = {@expr@} \), and write:

\[ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = {@ev(L1s,simp=false)@} = {@buggy_final@}. \][[/ if ]] [[ if test="notn=3" ]]

They want \( \dfrac{d}{dx}\!\left({@expr@}\right) \), and write:

\[ \dfrac{d}{dx}\!\left({@expr@}\right) = {@ev(L1s,simp=false)@} = {@buggy_final@}. \][[/ if ]]

(a)  What, if anything, is wrong with this working?

Bring the exponent \( {@n@} \) down as a multiplying factor and reduce the power to \( {@m@} \); the constant multiple \( {@c@} \) stays put.
